outline.chapter_title: Case Background, Charges, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the factual basis of the case, the defendant's criminal history, the charges brought under 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(e), the trial and conviction, and the scope of issues raised on appeal. It sets the stage for understanding why the district court made the rulings it did and why the Eighth Circuit reviewed them.
subtopics: The November 19-20, 2020 incident: Cutbank's methamphetamine use, holding D.F. at gunpoint, paranoid accusations, and physical abuse
Cutbank's flight with D.F.'s cell phone and the gun, and D.F.'s subsequent call to police
The police response to the garage call, Cutbank's barricading and resistance, including biting an officer and grabbing the officer's gun
Recovery of physical evidence along the path between D.F.'s home and the garage: the cell phone, butcher knife, and sawed-off Marlin .22 caliber rifle
DNA evidence linking Cutbank to the firearm and witness identifications of the weapon
Cutbank's extensive criminal history and the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) designation
The jury conviction for felon in possession and the finding of three prior violent felonies triggering § 924(e) enhanced penalties
The 292-month within-guidelines sentence and the two categories of issues on appeal: evidentiary/procedural errors and the USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) sentencing enhancement

outline.chapter_title: Evidentiary Issues I — Rule 404(b) and Prior Possession of the Same Firearm
outline.description: This chapter examines the defense's pretrial and trial objections to testimony that D.F. and C.F. had previously observed Cutbank with the same sawed-off Marlin .22 caliber rifle. It covers the distinction between propensity evidence barred by Rule 404(b) and intrinsic evidence admissible to prove an element of the charged offense, specifically possession.
subtopics: The pretrial motion to exclude D.F. and C.F. testimony under Rule 404(b) as propensity evidence
The government's counterargument that prior possession of the same weapon is intrinsic evidence relevant to proving the possession charge
The district court's pretrial ruling adopting the government's position

The Eighth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Battle: prior possession of a firearm is directly relevant to proving later possession of the same weapon because it helps establish ownership or control
The distinction between Rule 404(b) propensity evidence and intrinsic evidence of continuous possession
D.F.'s trial testimony that she had seen Cutbank with the sawed-off rifle a 'handful of times' before the incident
C.F.'s trial testimony that she had seen the gun 'once or twice' before and the defense's renewed objections
The Eighth Circuit's affirmation of the district court's ruling citing Battle and the lack of contrary authority from the defense

outline.chapter_title: Evidentiary Issues II — Hearsay, Confrontation Clause, Impeachment, and Harmless Error
outline.description: This chapter addresses the remaining evidentiary and procedural challenges: the defense's request for a limiting instruction on D.F.'s statements to police, Confrontation Clause concerns, the admission of testimony about D.F.'s sister being killed by a gun, limitations on cross-examination of C.F. regarding a police report, and the standards for harmless error and cumulative error review.
subtopics: The defense's pretrial request for a jury instruction limiting the use of D.F.'s statements to police until D.F. testified, to avoid hearsay and Confrontation Clause issues
The government's argument that officer testimony would establish context for their actions and knowledge at the time
The abuse of discretion standard for reviewing a district court's decision not to give a limiting instruction (United States v. Bennett)
The principle that a court need not give contemporaneous limiting instructions if an appropriate instruction is provided at the close of trial
Confrontation Clause satisfaction when the hearsay declarant appears and testifies in person (United States v. Charboneau)
The defense's motion to strike D.F.'s testimony that her sister was killed by a gun, offered in response to cross-examination about prior inconsistent statements
Rule 403 balancing: the absence of unfair prejudice or confusion from the sister testimony, and the district court's broad evidentiary discretion (Sprint/United Mgmt. Co. v. Mendelsohn)

The defense's attempt to cross-examine C.F. using a police report she did not author and the authentication requirement for extrinsic evidence of prior inconsistent statements (United States v. Cumbie)
The harmless error standard: reversal only if the jury may have been substantially swayed by improperly admitted evidence (United States v. DeMarce)
The cumulative error doctrine and the substantial evidence of guilt supporting the conviction (United States v. Keys)

outline.chapter_title: Sentencing — The § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancement and Sentence Reasonableness
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the sentencing phase of the case, including the Presentence Investigation Report's recommended offense level calculations, the four-level enhancement under USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) for possession of a firearm in connection with another felony, the interaction between the ACCA and the Armed Career Criminal Guideline, and the procedural and substantive reasonableness of the within-guidelines sentence.
subtopics: The PSR's recommended base offense level of 26 (sawed-off firearm plus two prior crimes of violence) and additional enhancements: three levels for altered serial number, two levels for reckless risk during flight, and four levels for possession in connection with another felony
The total offense level of 35 and Criminal History Category VI, yielding an advisory range of 292 to 365 months

The § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) enhancement standard: applies when a defendant used or possessed any firearm in connection with another felony offense, regardless of whether a charge was brought or conviction obtained (USSG § 2K2.1 comment. n.14(C))
The district court's adoption of PSR factual statements without objection and the clearly erroneous standard of review for factual findings (United States v. Dunn)
Cutbank's argument that the four-level enhancement conflicts with 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)'s 'sufficient, but not greater than necessary' principle
The interaction between the Armed Career Criminal Guideline (which would yield offense level 34) and the § 2K2.1 enhancement (level 35), with the greater offense level applying under USSG § 4B1.4(b)
Procedural reasonableness: the threshold requirement that the district court correctly calculate the applicable Guidelines range (Gall v. United States; Rosales-Mireles v. United States)
The presumption of reasonableness for within-guidelines sentences on appeal (United States v. Goodhouse)

The district court's consideration of § 3553(a) factors and the presumption that the court considered and rejected the defendant's variance arguments (United States v. Masood; United States v. Maluoth)

Substantive reasonableness analysis: the district court's substantial sentencing discretion, the aggravating facts of the offense (domestic abuse, kidnapping, assault in presence of children, injuring an officer), and the affirmance of the 292-month sentence
